checks.claim: Key: only all three in parallel leaves the other two lit whichever bulb is unscrewed (each parallel branch has its own path and the full voltage)
checks.note: Grokipedia: in parallel 'the voltage drop across each branch is equal to the total applied voltage'; 'If one appliance fails or is unplugged, the others continue to receive full voltage and operate normally.'

checks.claim: Wrong: all three in series (removing any one opens the only path, all go dark)
checks.note: Series: one path, 'The same current flows through each resistor in series'; Grokipedia: 'a failure or open circuit in any single component interrupts the entire path.'

checks.claim: Wrong: two in series with the third in parallel with that pair (unscrewing one of the pair puts out its partner)
checks.note: Worked out: removing a bulb of the series pair opens that branch, so its partner goes out; fails the stem.

checks.claim: Wrong: two in parallel with the third in series with them (unscrewing the series bulb puts out all three)
checks.note: Worked out: the series bulb carries the whole current; removing it opens the only path. Removing one of the parallel pair leaves the other two lit, but the stem says whichever bulb, so it fails.

checks.claim: Context: in each arrangement all three light first (series pair dimmer, but lit)
checks.note: Every arrangement is a closed path through every bulb, so all three light, as the stem says.

checks.claim: Context: old strings of holiday lights were series, one bulb out and all go dark
checks.note: Grokipedia: older series strings, 'the failure of one bulb interrupts current flow to the entire chain.' 'Old' keeps it true of modern shunted sets.

checks.claim: Stem: lamps and sockets in a house are wired in parallel
checks.note: OpenStax: car devices 'are wired in parallel, so that they utilize the full voltage of the source'; 'The same is true in your house, or any building.' Grokipedia: 'outlets are wired in parallel to provide the standard line voltage.'

checks.claim: Key: so each gets the full voltage and works alone
checks.note: Grokipedia: parallel allows 'independent use without one device affecting the voltage or operation of another.'

checks.claim: Wrong: so each gets an equal share of the voltage (that is series: the voltage is divided)
checks.note: OpenStax: 'Individual resistors in series do not get the total source voltage, but divide it.' In parallel each gets the full voltage, not a share.

checks.claim: Wrong: so the house draws less current (parallel branches add current)
checks.note: Grokipedia: parallel resistors reduce equivalent resistance, 'thereby increasing the total current drawn from the source'; OpenStax: total current is 'the sum of these currents.'

checks.claim: Wrong: so a fault in one lamp cuts off all the others
checks.note: The opposite of the reason; that is the series failure mode.

checks.claim: Context: each branch switched on draws its own current, so more in all
Stem: an ammeter reads current, the flow of charge, in amperes
Key: the same reading either side of the bulb; no charge is used up
checks.note: Illinois Q&A: if the current leaving were smaller, charge would pile up in the bulb; the current is the same on both sides. UK Power Networks and Oak National Academy: the reading is the same wherever the ammeter sits in a series loop; current is not 'used up'. OpenStax 20.2: 'the same q flows through each.'

checks.claim: Wrong: lower leaving, the bulb uses up some current (the classic consumption misconception)
checks.note: Named misconception; IOP diagnostic questions also use 'some of the current is used up by the bulb' as the wrong answer.

checks.claim: Wrong: lower leaving, some charge becomes light
checks.note: The bulb converts energy (OpenStax: 'the resistor converts it to another form'), not charge.

checks.claim: Wrong: higher leaving, the bulb speeds the charge up
checks.note: Charge conservation: same current in and out.

checks.claim: Context: the bulb takes energy carried by the moving charge; the battery supplies energy, not a store of current
checks.note: Fine at grade level (the source supplies energy, the resistor converts it).

checks.claim: Key: on the same voltage the 60 W bulb draws more current, so it has less resistance than the 25 W bulb
checks.note: OpenStax: 'Since both operate on the same voltage, the 60-W bulb must draw more current to have a greater power rating. Thus the 60-W bulb's resistance must be lower than that of a 25-W bulb.'

checks.claim: Wrong: it has more resistance (the named misconception)
checks.note: OpenStax: 'the lower the resistance connected to a given voltage source, the greater the power delivered.'

checks.claim: Wrong: it gets more voltage (house sockets are parallel, same full voltage)
Wrong: it holds more charge (a filament stores no charge)
Context: 'with the same push more current flows only where there is less resistance: that is Ohm's law in words'
checks.note: Acceptable at grade level: R = V/I at the operating point, which is how OpenStax treats bulbs. Strictly a filament lamp is non-ohmic (Grokipedia: Ohm's law 'does not hold for ... filament lamps'), so a pedant could object to 'Ohm's law'. Optional tightening: '...less resistance: that is what resistance means.'

checks.claim: Ohm taught in Cologne (Jesuit Gymnasium, from 1817)
checks.note: Grokipedia and MacTutor: Jesuit Gymnasium of Cologne from 1817; DSB: leave in Berlin from August 1826.

checks.claim: He sent currents through wires of different lengths and thicknesses
checks.note: DSB: the 1825 paper used one 'very thick' wire four inches long and six thinner ones of one to seventy-five feet. Grokipedia: wires of varying lengths, diameters and materials.

checks.claim: Book of 1827 (Die galvanische Kette, mathematisch bearbeitet) tied current to the push and to resistance
Quote: 'Critics in Germany called it "a web of naked fancies."'
checks.note: The words are documented as one reviewer's, not critics' in the plural. Popular Science Monthly (1913), from H. W. Dove: the theory 'was named a web of naked fancies' in the Berlin Jahrbucher fur wissenschaftliche Kritik (the journal that carried G. F. Pohl's 1828 review, per the DSB and the Deutsches Museum archive). The English goes back to Tyndall's 1852 report, which calls the reviewer 'the writer' (via Hart, Makers of Science, 1924). Wikipedia says 'critics' with no primary source; Grokipedia names Schweigger, who in fact printed Ohm's papers. FIX: 'A reviewer in a Berlin journal called it "a web of naked fancies."' Name no one, since Pohl is likely but not documented.

checks.claim: Gustav Fechner tested the rule carefully in 1831 and his results agreed
checks.note: DSB: in Massbestimmungen uber die galvanische Kette (1831) Fechner 'subjected it to rigorous experimental testing (and confirmation).'

checks.claim: Key: twice the push and the same current in one wire would count against Ohm
checks.note: I proportional to V for an ohmic wire, so doubling V with no change in I breaks the law.

checks.claim: Wrong choices all fit Ohm: twice push and twice current; same push and less current in a longer wire; same push and more current in a thicker wire
checks.note: Resistance is proportional to length and inversely to cross-sectional area (same metal implied).

checks.claim: Context: the quarrel was mostly with treating electricity by mathematics, which most German physicists did not do
checks.note: MacTutor and the DSB: the older German physicists were not convinced the mathematical approach was right; Pohl complained that Ohm only put properties of electricity into formulas.

checks.claim: Context: Copley Medal from the Royal Society in 1841; resistance measured in ohms
checks.note: Grokipedia: Copley Medal 1841; the ohm was adopted in 1881. DSB: 30 November 1841.

checks.claim: Faraday a blacksmith's son with only basic schooling
checks.note: Grokipedia: father 'a blacksmith originally from Yorkshire'; Sunday school basics. Wikipedia: 'only the most basic school education.'

checks.claim: Apprenticed to a London bookbinder at fourteen; read the books in the shop
checks.note: Grokipedia: in 1805, at 14, a seven-year apprenticeship under George Riebau in London. (Faraday wrote that he entered the shop at 13 in 1804, as errand boy; the formal apprenticeship came at 14.)

checks.claim: He wrote long after (letter to De La Rive, 2 October 1858) that Marcet's Conversations on Chemistry gave him his foundation in that science
checks.note: Letter: 'Mrs. Marcets conversations on chemistry ... gave me my foundation in that science.'

checks.claim: Key: he tested her claims with little experiments of his own
checks.note: Letter: tested 'by such little experiments as I could find means to perform.'

checks.claim: Wrong choices (took on trust; waited for a chemist to vouch; learned by heart untested) all contradicted by the letter
checks.note: 'I could trust a fact,- but always cross examined an assertion.'

checks.claim: Context quotes: 'I could trust a fact ... cross examined an assertion'; 'such little experiments as I could find means to perform'; 'got hold of an anchor in chemical knowledge' (felt when the book agreed with his tests)
checks.note: All three are in the letter as quoted. The anchor came when he found the book matched the facts as far as he could tell.

checks.claim: Context: in 1812 he heard Davy lecture at the Royal Institution
checks.note: The RI and Faraday's 1829 letter to Paris say these were Davy's last lectures there.

checks.claim: Context: he sent Davy 'a book of about 300 pages' made from his notes
checks.note: The sources disagree: Wikipedia says 300 pages, Grokipedia 313, and Bence Jones (who had the volume at the RI) 386 small quarto pages, as cited in search results; I could not open the Bence Jones text itself. The fact sheet puts the page count under Left out, yet the context uses it. FIX: drop the number: 'sent him a bound book made from his notes' (Faraday's 1829 letter to Paris: he wrote the notes out 'more fairly in a quarto volume').

checks.claim: Context: on 1 March 1813 Davy took him on as his chemical assistant
checks.note: Grokipedia: Davy appointed him 'his chemical assistant at the Royal Institution on March 1, 1813'; Wikipedia: appointed Chemical Assistant at the RI on 1 March 1813.

checks.claim: Stem: September 1821 at the Royal Institution; magnet upright in a deep basin of mercury, its top just above the surface; wire hung from above, lower end in the mercury; current down the wire
checks.note: RI: 3 September 1821; the notebook for 4 September has 'A deep basin with a bit of wax at bottom and then filled with mercury', 'a magnet stuck upright in wax so that pole just above surface of mercury', a wire 'at lower end dipping into mercury'.

checks.claim: Key: the wire circled the magnet while the current ran
checks.note: Notebook: 'the revolution of the wire round the pole of the magnet.'

checks.claim: Wrong: swung onto the magnet and clung; swung away and hung; twitched once then hung still
checks.note: The force is perpendicular to both current and field, so the motion is a continuous circling, not attraction, repulsion or a single twitch.

checks.claim: Context: the push is at right angles to both the current and the field, so the wire is shoved sideways, never pulled in; the mercury kept the circuit whole
checks.note: True for this straight wire beside a pole.

checks.claim: Context: 'It was the first electric motor, the first steady motion ever made from electricity'
checks.note: The RI says 'world's first electric motor' and 'for the first time, continuous mechanical movement was generated from electricity'; Grokipedia calls it 'the first primitive electric motor'. But Wikipedia: 'The first electric motors were simple electrostatic devices' (Andrew Gordon, Benjamin Franklin, 1740s-1750s), and Franklin's electric wheel turned steadily. FIX: 'It was the first electromagnetic motor, the first steady motion made from a current and a magnet.'

checks.claim: Context: 'every motor since turns on the same sideways push, with a coil in place of the wire'
checks.note: Not every motor. Grokipedia: in switched reluctance motors 'torque is produced by aligning rotor poles with energized stator poles' (a pull on iron, no current in the rotor), and piezoelectric motors 'operate without magnetic fields'. Wikipedia: motors work on 'magnetism, electrostatics and piezoelectricity'. FIX: 'and most motors since, in fans, drills and cars, turn on the same sideways push, with a coil in place of the wire.'

checks.claim: Stem: 29 August 1831, two separate coils on opposite sides of an iron ring, one to a battery, the other to a galvanometer
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'On August 29, 1831, Faraday achieved his first success with what became known as the ring experiment.' Grokipedia (Michael Faraday): iron ring with two insulated copper coils, galvanometer. (In the diary the second coil's wire ran over a magnetic needle, which amounts to a simple galvanometer.)

checks.claim: Key: the needle moved only as the battery was joined or broken
checks.note: 'Upon completing or breaking the battery circuit, Faraday observed transient deflections'; 'no effect occurred during steady current flow.'

checks.claim: Wrong: all the while the current flowed; once the ring grew warm; after a few minutes
checks.note: OpenStax: 'if the switch remains closed or open for any length of time, there is no current through the galvanometer.'

checks.claim: Context: one way on joining and the other on breaking; still while the current was steady
checks.note: The deflections were 'reversing direction based on whether the circuit was made or broken.'

checks.claim: Context: earlier tries with steady currents and magnets at rest had found nothing
checks.note: 'Early attempts by Faraday to induce currents using static magnets or steady electric currents yielded no results.'

checks.claim: Context: Joseph Henry in Albany found it on his own; published 1832; credit generally to Faraday
checks.note: Henry 'independently observed the phenomenon' at the Albany Academy; credit generally goes to Faraday for earlier presentation and publication; Henry published in 1832 in the American Journal of Science (Grokipedia, Electromagnetic induction).

checks.claim: Stem: later in 1831 Faraday pushed a bar magnet into a coil joined to a galvanometer; flick in, zero at rest, flick the other way out
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'later that year' he moved a bar magnet in and out of a coil connected to a galvanometer; currents appeared only during motion. OpenStax: no emf when the magnet is still; reversing the motion reverses it.

checks.claim: Key: only a changing magnetic field makes a current
checks.note: The standard grade-level statement, true here, where the magnet moves and the coil stands still. Strictly it is a change in the field THROUGH THE COIL (flux), as the context goes on to say. Optional tightening: 'Only a changing field through the coil makes a current.'

checks.claim: Wrong: only a moving magnet has a field; motion rubs charge off the wire; the magnet carries charge in
checks.note: A still magnet keeps its field; induction is not friction or carried charge.

checks.claim: Context: moving the coil past a still magnet works as well; a quicker push gives a bigger flick
checks.note: Deflections 'proportional to the speed of motion'; moving the coil past fixed poles 'yielded comparable results'.

checks.claim: Context: 'Every generator works this way: something keeps the field through its coils changing'
checks.note: Not every generator. Faraday's own disc of October 1831, the homopolar generator, has no coils and gives a steady current with 'a radial EMF despite no apparent flux change through a fixed circuit' (Grokipedia); it is the textbook exception to the flux rule. Electrostatic generators also work otherwise. FIX: 'The generators in power stations work this way: their turbines keep the field through the coils changing.' (Grokipedia, Electric generator: turbines spin the rotor inside the stator windings.)

checks.claim: Key: easing off the pedal, the motor works as a generator charging the battery (regenerative braking)
checks.note: Grokipedia: kinetic energy is converted 'into electrical energy, which is stored in a battery'; the motor switches to generator mode; 'releasing the accelerator pedal engages motor-generated drag'.

checks.claim: Wrong: working as a motor, pushing back on battery power
checks.note: In regeneration energy flows into the battery, not out of it.

checks.claim: Wrong: a brake rubbing on its own shaft; a magnet gripping the steel axle
checks.note: Neither is how it works; friction braking is the separate pad brake.

checks.claim: Context: friction brakes still needed for a full stop, because the effect fades at low speed
checks.note: Grokipedia: regeneration 'becomes ineffective at low speeds, typically below 5-10 km/h'; blended with friction brakes.

checks.claim: Context: 1873, Hippolyte Fontaine, by accident, wired an idle Gramme machine to a working one and its shaft began to spin
checks.note: Wikipedia: Fontaine 'carelessly connected the terminals of a Gramme machine to another dynamo which was producing electricity', and 'its shaft began to spin'. Grokipedia: he 'accidentally connected two machines via a long cable' (Vienna, the second driving a pump). The Wikipedia Fontaine page gives the distance as two kilometres, Grokipedia about 500 m; the question gives none.

checks.claim: Context: 'One machine turns electricity into motion or motion into electricity, as Hippolyte Fontaine found by accident in 1873'
checks.note: 'Found' reads as discovering it first, and that is disputed. Wikipedia (Electric motor): 'the discovery of the reversibility of the electric machine, which was announced by Siemens in 1867 and observed by Pacinotti', and Gramme 'accidentally demonstrated it' at Vienna in 1873; Wikipedia (Pacinotti): he 'found that the device could also be used as an electric motor' (built 1860, published 1865). Grokipedia and Britannica credit Fontaine with revealing or discovering it. FIX: '...as Hippolyte Fontaine showed by accident at Vienna in 1873, when...'. 'Showed' is true on every account.

unit_notes: Physics questions 1-4 are sound; I worked out the three-bulb arrangements independently and they match the context. The faults are in the history and in claims with 'every': (1) Q5 puts one reviewer's phrase, in a Berlin journal and probably Pohl's 1828 review, in the mouths of 'critics'; (2) Q7 'every motor since' is false (reluctance and piezo motors), and 'first steady motion ever made from electricity' clashes with Wikipedia's 1740s electrostatic motors; (3) Q9 'every generator' is false, Faraday's own homopolar disc being the classic exception; (4) Q6's page count is disputed (300, 313 or 386) and the fact sheet itself lists it as left out; (5) Q10 'Fontaine found' should be 'showed', since Siemens (1867) and Pacinotti had already noted reversibility. Every quotation in Q6 is verbatim in Faraday's letter of 2 October 1858. Nothing here goes out of date over time.
